newsitem.title: USA: Niagara Mohawk sees improved credit rating.
newsitem.headline: Niagara Mohawk sees improved credit rating.

text.p: Niagara Mohawk Power Corp expects its settlement with independent power producers will allow it to seek an investment grade rating on its senior debt by year 2000, chief executive William E. Davis said Monday.
The goal was announced during a teleconference describing the settlement to analysts, who questioned it as "aggressive."

Calling the tentative agreement a "leveraged recapitalization of the company," Davis said the goal is based on the delevering expected over the first three years of the agreement, adding the utility's cash flow status is more supportive of the change than its capital status.
Although the cash flow will be strengthened, Davis said in conclusion of the teleconference, the booked (or reported) net (income) of the company will be reduced as a result" of the settlement.
He did not elaborate on this projection.
Davis said the debt to be issued as a result of the settlement will be less than investment grade.

Mike Ranger of Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette said the $3.6 billion of debt and cash will include $3.2 billion of debt and $400 million of cash with some of the $3.2 billion "to be sold into the market" to fund additional cash payments.
Noting Niagara Mohawk said the debt would be subordinate to its first mortgage bonds, Ranger said the new debt may still have some security attached.
He said the cash would come from the company's net operating loss carryforward, which is expected to provide $250 million, and cash on hand, which is expected to total $270 million by year end.
Ranger said the debt will be distribution company debt if the proposed restructuring of Niagara Mohawk is approved by regulators.

Noting the fininancing is now expected to go to market after the end this year's of New York state legislative session, Davis said approval of the pending stranded asset securitization legislation would "enhance the deal" reached with the IPPs, creating a chance for rate cuts beyond the undisclosed cuts envisioned by the agreement.
Ranger said the agreement will create a regulatory asset of "about $4 billion" which will be amortized over 10 years.
The tentative agreements cover about 2,000 megawatts of contracted power, Niagara Mohawk's Mike Kelleher said.
Davis said the proposed agreement calls for buyout out about half of the power contracts.
Of the rest, which use natural gas as a fuel, he said the utility expects to negotiate fixed price contracts with 40 percent and have the price of power from the rest based on natural gas prices.
He said directors will make decisions on the company's first quarter preferred dividends and closing the books on 1996 at this week's scheduled board meeting.
"There are no other significant write-downs contemplated" for 1996, Davis said.

The proposed IPP agreement meets the goals of New York Public Service Commission Chairman John O'Mara, Davis noted, adding "It's fair to say we've hgad a lot of discussions with Chairman O'Mara and the senior staff along the way."
Davis also said the company believes the commission has the power to approve the proposal without legislative action.
He concluded the teleconference calling the proposal "a major accomplishment ... that provides the company with a much more positive outlook."
